prompt:
An engineering org is frustrated that pull requests sit in review too long — median time-to-first-review is 9 hours and leadership believes this is the main drag on delivery. They introduce a policy: every PR must receive its first review within 2 hours, and each engineer's individual performance score now includes a "review responsiveness" metric based on how quickly they respond to review requests. The stated goal is to ship features faster without sacrificing quality. In the first three weeks, median time-to-first-review drops to 40 minutes and dashboards look great; leadership declares the initiative a success and plans to expand it.

Reviewers, now measured on speed, adapt: they clear their review queue quickly to protect their score, which in practice means approving large PRs with a skim and an "LGTM," deferring genuinely hard reviews, and nudging authors toward larger batched PRs that are faster to rubber-stamp than many small ones. The metric rewards fast clicks, not careful reading. Considering the full chain of consequences — how the people being measured will adapt, and what happens to defect escape rate, production incidents, and downstream rework once review becomes a formality — decide whether this policy will ACHIEVE its stated goal of shipping faster without sacrificing quality, or whether second-order effects (gamed metric, degraded review depth, more escaped defects and rework) will undermine or reverse that goal even though the first-order review-time number improves.
decision_instruction: Consider the full chain of consequences of the proposed action, not just the immediate effect. Answer YES if, accounting for second- and third-order effects (feedback, incentives, adaptation by others), the action will ACHIEVE its stated goal. Answer NO if downstream/second-order effects will UNDERMINE or reverse the stated goal even though the first-order effect looks positive.

prompt:
A write-heavy API endpoint collapses during traffic spikes: when load exceeds the database's capacity, every request slows down, clients hit their timeouts and immediately retry, the retries pile on more load, and the whole endpoint enters a death spiral where almost no request succeeds. The infra team proposes what sounds counterintuitive: add an admission-control concurrency limiter in front of the database that caps in-flight writes at a level empirically below the database's saturation point, and immediately reject (fast `503` with `Retry-After`) any request beyond that cap instead of queueing it. Deliberately serving fewer requests at once, and outright refusing some, is expected to INCREASE the number of requests that ultimately succeed during a spike.

The reasoning draws on queueing theory: holding concurrency below saturation keeps per-request latency under the client timeout, so accepted requests actually complete instead of timing out; fast rejection with backoff prevents the retry-amplification feedback loop; and total successful throughput (goodput) rises even though instantaneous accepted concurrency falls. A skeptic objects: "Throttling and rejecting requests obviously reduces how many you serve — you can't increase successful requests by handling fewer of them." Considering the second-order dynamics (client retry behavior, the timeout/latency relationship, and feedback under overload), decide whether adding the concurrency limiter with fast rejection will ACHIEVE its stated goal of increasing the number of requests that successfully complete during spikes, or whether it will undermine that goal.

Answer YES if, accounting for second- and third-order effects (feedback, incentives, adaptation by others), the action will ACHIEVE its stated goal. prompt:
A platform team is under pressure to cut cloud spend. They notice a fleet of ~30 internal microservices sitting mostly idle between bursts of activity, and propose configuring aggressive scale-to-zero: after 60 seconds with no requests, each service scales its instances down to zero, spinning back up on the next request. A month-one projection shows roughly a 30% reduction in compute cost, and leadership approves it as a clean win with the stated goal of durably lowering infrastructure cost without harming reliability or user-facing performance.

The wrinkle is in how these services actually receive traffic. They are not user-idle; they exchange frequent, bursty, latency-sensitive calls with each other in short clustered waves — a request to service A fans out to eight downstream services, several of which have just scaled to zero and now incur multi-second cold starts (container pull, runtime init, dependency warm-up, connection re-establishment). Cold-start stampedes cause cascading timeouts and retries; retries generate more traffic that repeatedly re-triggers scale-up and scale-down cycles; on-call load and SLA breaches rise; and teams start pinning minimum instance counts back up or adding keep-alive pingers to dodge cold starts. Considering the full chain of second-order effects (cold-start latency, retry amplification, thrashing between scale-up and scale-down, and how teams adapt), decide whether aggressive scale-to-zero will ACHIEVE its stated goal of durably lowering cost without harming reliability or performance, or whether downstream effects will undermine or reverse it.
decision_instruction: Consider the full chain of consequences of the proposed action, not just the immediate effect. Answer YES if, accounting for second- and third-order effects (feedback, incentives, adaptation by others), the action will ACHIEVE its stated goal. Answer NO if downstream/second-order effects will UNDERMINE or reverse the stated goal even though the first-order effect looks positive.

prompt:
A team's CI signal has become worthless: the main test suite fails on roughly 40% of runs due to accumulated flaky tests, so engineers now reflexively hit "re-run" on any red build and merge once it happens to go green. Real regressions slip through because nobody trusts or reads the failures anymore. The team proposes a quarantine policy: any test that flakes is moved out of the blocking suite into a separate non-blocking "quarantine" suite that still runs and reports but cannot block a merge; a named owner is assigned to each quarantined test with a one-week SLA to fix or delete it; and a hard cap limits how many tests may sit in quarantine at once, so the queue cannot grow unbounded. The stated goal is to restore a trustworthy blocking signal so that a red main build once again means a genuine regression that engineers stop and investigate.

A skeptic warns: "Quarantining flaky tests is just sweeping problems under the rug — you'll lose coverage and the quarantine will become a graveyard nobody looks at." Considering the second-order effects — how engineers respond to a green build that once again means something, whether owned SLAs plus a hard cap actually keep the quarantine from becoming a dumping ground, and the net effect on caught regressions — decide whether this quarantine-with-ownership policy will ACHIEVE its stated goal of restoring a trustworthy blocking CI signal, or whether downstream effects will undermine it.
